builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
summary: Intent contracts replace planner-written tool calls (optionally screened by a reviewer) with a logged goal-plus-quotation contract that validation code and a small trusted model convert into the actual tool call, confining the planner's influence to the contract. The cost is an extra trusted-model call per step, additional validation and dispatch code whose correctness the guarantees depend on, and the need to structure every action as a contract. It can fail on ambiguous references: once environment terms are clarified, state-changing conditions hit a wrong target in 40-49% of runs, because the trusted model cannot see the environment to check object choice, and it does not reduce unauthorized actions compared with blind review.
rationale: The mechanism is implementable with existing APIs and a small trusted model, but the paper shows it fails to prevent wrong-target actions from ambiguous references, so it warrants workload-specific validation rather than direct adoption as a safety control.

claims.statement: Intent contracts replace planner-written tool calls (optionally screened by a reviewer) with a logged goal-plus-quotation contract that validation code and a small trusted model convert into the actual tool call, confining the planner's influence to the contract. The cost is an extra trusted-model call per step, additional validation and dispatch code whose correctness the guarantees depend on, and the need to structure every action as a contract. It can fail on ambiguous references: once environment terms are clarified, state-changing conditions hit a wrong target in 40-49% of runs, because the trusted model cannot see the environment to check object choice, and it does not reduce unauthorized actions compared with blind review.

When the planner adds unrequested work, intent contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs versus 16/30 for an intent-visible command reviewer; contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions relative to blind review.
